recipe.history:
Okra — Abelmoschus esculentus — is a flowering plant in the mallow family, native to the region spanning Ethiopia and the Sudan, where it has been cultivated for at least two thousand years and possibly much longer. The ancient Egyptians grew it along the Nile, and it spread along trade routes and migration paths through North Africa, the Middle East, and eventually into the Mediterranean. It arrived in the Americas on slave ships during the horrific forced migration of the transatlantic slave trade, carried by enslaved Africans who brought seeds as both sustenance and cultural connection to the lands from which they had been violently removed. In this way, okra became one of the most consequential ingredients in the history of American cooking — not as a curiosity or an import, but as a survival food that became a cornerstone of Southern and Gulf Coast cuisine. Its mucilaginous quality, the characteristic stickiness that so many people find off-putting, was recognized by West African and Creole cooks as a thickening agent of remarkable power, making it the indispensable base of gumbo, one of America's most complex and beloved dishes.

Fried okra — okra dredged in seasoned cornmeal or flour and deep-fried until the exterior is shatteringly crisp while the interior remains tender and only slightly sticky — became a staple of Southern cooking as a way to celebrate the vegetable while managing its texture for those unfamiliar with it. It translated to burger culture as part of the broader movement to incorporate Southern ingredients and techniques into American comfort food. Fried okra strips on a burger add a dimension of texture that nothing else can provide: the crunch of the cornmeal crust, the slight resistance of the vegetable beneath, the clean grassy-slightly-sweet flavor of okra itself that differs from any fried vegetable substitute. An okra relish — cooked down with vinegar, tomato, and spices — provides the counterpoint of soft, acidic, lightly spiced vegetable against the crunch of the fried strips.

I spent a summer in Louisiana in my late twenties, and okra was everywhere: in gumbo, fried beside catfish, pickled and served alongside cold drinks on porches in the early evenings. A woman named Deloris, who ran a small catering operation out of her home kitchen, fried okra in a cast-iron pot that she said had belonged to her grandmother, and the okra came out with a cornmeal crust so light and so shattering that it bore no relationship to any fried vegetable I had encountered before. She served it simply, with hot sauce and salt, and I ate an embarrassing amount of it. When I came home I tried for months to replicate that crust, and when I finally got close to it I immediately put it on a burger, because putting something on a burger is how I understand what it is. The okra understood.

Fried okra on a burger is one of those toppings that changes your relationship with the internal temperature of the patty, because the textural contrast it provides — crackingly crisp crust, yielding vegetable — requires a medium rare counterpart to be fully understood. A well-done patty is also dense and dry, and placing fried okra on top of it produces a burger that is all resistance, all chew, nothing that yields. A medium rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit offers that yielding quality — the softness of properly cooked muscle, the liquidity of still-warm fat — that makes the crunch of the fried okra sing by contrast. The medium rare patty is the soft note that makes the crisp note worth hearing.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
300g fresh okra, caps trimmed, sliced lengthwise into halves
1 clove garlic, minced to a paste
2 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
instructions: 1. Make the remoulade: Whisk together mayonnaise, both mustards, hot sauce, lemon juice, Worcestershire, garlic paste, parsley, celery, and smoked paprika until smooth and well combined. Season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate at least 30 minutes.

2. Make the okra relish: Heat olive oil in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add yellow onion and cook 3–4 minutes until softened. Add okra rounds, tomato, apple cider vinegar, sugar, red pepper flakes, and salt. Cook, stirring, for 10–12 minutes until okra is tender and the liquid has reduced to a light syrup. Cool to room temperature.

3. Make the bun dough: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg. Mix on medium with the dough hook for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
4. Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.
5. Divide into 4 equal portions. Shape into smooth balls, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 45 minutes.
6. Brush with egg wash and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool on a wire rack.

7. Prepare the okra for frying: Soak the sliced okra halves in a shallow dish with buttermilk and hot sauce for 20 minutes. Whisk together cornmeal, flour, salt, smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, cayenne, and black pepper in a bowl.

8. Fry the okra: Heat 2 inches of neutral oil in a heavy pot to 350°F (175°C). Working in batches, lift okra pieces from the buttermilk, dredge well in the cornmeal mixture, and fry for 2–3 minutes until deep golden and crisp. Transfer to a wire rack. Season immediately with salt.

9. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions of about 170g each. Form into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and Cajun seasoning. Refrigerate 15 minutes.
10. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side without pressing. Flip and cook 2–3 minutes second side.
11. Lay a slice of pepper jack on each patty. Add a splash of water, cover immediately, and steam 30–45 seconds until cheese is melted.
12. Transfer patties to a resting rack and rest 3–4 minutes. Target internal temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
13. Split and toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1–2 minutes.

14. Assemble: Spread remoulade generously on both cut surfaces of each bun. Place lettuce and tomato slices on the bottom bun. Set the cheesed patty on top. Spoon okra relish over the patty. Stack a generous pile of fried okra strips on top of the relish. Finish with flaky sea salt. Set the top bun in place and serve immediately while the okra is still hot and crisp.
